title: Those who truly bear the name of Christian
source_text: Καὶ οὔπω λέγω τὰ λοιπὰ ἐν ἀνθρώποις κακὰ, ὧν οὐ ταχέως οὐδ᾿ οἱ φιλοσοφεῖν δοκοῦντες καθαρεύουσι (πολλοὶ γὰρ καὶ οἱ ἐν φιλοσοφίᾳ νόθοι) οὐδέ φημι πὼ ὅτι πολλὰ μέν ἐστι τὰ τοιαῦτα παρὰ τοῖς μήτε Ἰουδαίοις μήτε Χριστιανοῖς· ἤτοι δὲ οὐδ᾿ ὅλως ὑπάρχει ἐν Χριστιανοῖς, εἰ κυρίως ἐξετάζοις, τίς ὁ Χριστιανὸς, ἢ εἰ καὶ εὑρεθείη, ἀλλ᾿ οὔτι γε ἐν τοῖς συνεδρεύουσι καὶ ἐπὶ τὰς κοινὰς εὐχὰς ἐρχομένοις καὶ μὴ ἀποκλειομένοις ἀπ᾿ αὐτῶν· εἰ μὴ ἄρα τις σπανίως λανθάνων ἐν τοῖς πολλοῖς εὑρίσκοιτο τοιοῦτος. οὐ σκώληκες οὖν ἐκκλησιάζοντές ἐσμεν οἱ πρὸς Ἰουδαίους ἱστάμενοι ἀπὸ τῶν πεπιστευμένων αὐτοῖς εἶναι γραμμάτων ἱερῶν καὶ δεικνύντες τόν τε προφητευόμενον ἐπιδεδημηκέναι καὶ διὰ τὰ μέγιστα ἁμαρτήματα ἐκείνους ἐγκαταλελεῖφθαι καὶ ἡμᾶς, τοὺς παραδεξαμένους τὸν λόγον, ἐλπίδας ἔχειν παρὰ θεῷ τὰς ἀρίστας ἔκ τε τῆς εἰς αὐτὸν πίστεως καὶ τοῦ δυναμένου ἡμᾶς οἰκειῶσαι αὐτῷ καθαροὺς ἀπὸ πάσης πονηρίας καὶ κακίας βίου. οὐχ ἁπλῶς οὖν, εἴ τις Ἰουδαῖον ἑαυτὸν ἢ Χριστιανὸν ἀναγορεύει, οὗτος λέγοι ἂν ὅτι τὸν πάντα κόσμον καὶ τὴν οὐράνιον φορὰν ἡμῖν μάλιστα πεποίηκεν ὁ θεός. ἀλλ᾿ εἴ τις, ὡς ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἐδίδαξε, καθαρός ἐστι „τῇ καρδίᾳ“ καὶ πρᾷος καὶ εἰρηνοποιὸς καὶ προθύμως ὑπομένων τοὺς διὰ τὴν εὐσέβειαν κινδύνους, εὐλόγως ἂν ὁ τοιοῦτος θαῤῥοίη τῷ θεῷ, συνιεὶς δὲ καὶ τὸν ἐν ταῖς προφητείαις λόγον φήσαι ἂν καὶ τό· πάντα ταῦτα ἡμῖν τοῖς πιστεύουσιν ὁ θεὸς προδεδήλωκε καὶ κατήγγειλεν.
pass_a_gloss: And not yet (οὔπω) do I speak of the remaining evils (κακά) among men, from which not quickly (ταχέως) are even those seeming to philosophise (φιλοσοφέω) clean (καθαρεύω) (for many are also the bastards/spurious (νόθος) in philosophy); nor do I yet say that many such things are among those neither Jews nor Christians; but either (ἤτοι) they do not exist at all among Christians, if you were to examine strictly (κυρίως) who the Christian is, or, if one were even found, yet certainly not (οὔτι γε) among those who sit together in council (συνεδρεύω) and come to the common prayers (κοιναὶ εὐχαί) and are not excluded (ἀποκλείω) from them; unless perhaps someone such were found rarely (σπανίως) escaping notice (λανθάνω) among the many. Not worms, then, holding assembly (ἐκκλησιάζω) are we who stand (ἵσταμαι) against Jews from the writings (γράμματα) believed by them to be sacred (ἱερός), and showing that the one prophesied (προφητεύω) has come to dwell (ἐπιδημέω), and that because of the greatest sins (ἁμάρτημα) they have been forsaken (ἐγκαταλείπω), and that we, who have received (παραδέχομαι) the word (λόγος), have the best hopes (ἐλπίδες ἄρισται) with God, both from faith (πίστις) in him and from a life (βίος) able to make us his own (οἰκειόω), pure from all wickedness (πονηρία) and vice (κακία). Not simply (ἁπλῶς), then, if someone proclaims (ἀναγορεύω) himself Jew or Christian, would this one say that the whole world (κόσμος) and the heavenly revolution (οὐράνιος φορά) God has made most of all (μάλιστα) for us. But if someone, as Jesus taught, is pure ‘in heart’ (καρδία) and meek (πρᾶος) and peacemaker (εἰρηνοποιός) and eagerly (προθύμως) enduring (ὑπομένω) the dangers (κίνδυνος) on account of piety, reasonably (εὐλόγως) would such a one be confident (θαρρέω) toward God; and understanding (συνίημι) also the meaning (λόγος) in the prophecies (προφητεία), he would say also this: all these things God has shown beforehand (προδηλόω) and announced (καταγγέλλω) to us who believe.
pass_b_english: And I do not yet speak of the other evils found among human beings, from which not even those who are reputed to be philosophers are readily free (for in philosophy too there are many counterfeits). Nor do I yet say that such evils abound among those who are neither Jews nor Christians, while among Christians they either do not exist at all, if you examine strictly who the Christian is, or, if they should be found, are certainly not found among those who meet together, come to the common prayers, and are not shut out from them; unless perhaps, on rare occasions, someone of that sort is found escaping notice among the many.

So we are not worms holding assembly, we who take our stand against the Jews on the basis of the writings they believe to be sacred, and who show that the one who was prophesied has come; that they have been forsaken because of their very great sins; and that we who have received the word have the best hopes with God, both from our faith in him and from a life that is able to make us, pure from all wickedness and vice, his own.

It is not, then, simply anyone who proclaims himself a Jew or a Christian who could say that God made the whole world and the motion of the heavens chiefly for us. But if someone is, as Jesus taught, pure “in heart” (Matthew 5:8), meek (Matthew 5:5), a peacemaker (Matthew 5:9), and one who readily endures dangers for the sake of piety (Matthew 5:10–11), such a person might with good reason have confidence in God; and, understanding the meaning of the prophecies as well, he might also say that God has shown all these things beforehand and announced them to us who believe.

choices.choice: τὸν προφητευόμενον: removed added 'by the prophets' -> 'the one who was prophesied'
καθαρούς agrees with ἡμᾶς: 'a life that is able to make us, pure from all wickedness and vice, his own' (was ambiguous, read as describing the life)
θαρροίη τῷ θεῷ: 'have confidence before God' -> 'have confidence in God'
Translator note added on the καθαρούς agreement

The Beatitude cluster (pure in heart, meek, peacemaker, enduring persecution for piety) is introduced by ‘as Jesus taught’; only καρδίᾳ is marked as quotation in the edition, the other three are allusions, each cited to its verse. ‘Holding assembly’ (ἐκκλησιάζοντες) and ‘the whole world and the motion of the heavens’ and ‘God has shown all these things beforehand and announced them’ deliberately echo Celsus’s words quoted in 4.23 (σκώληξιν ἐν βορβόρου γωνίᾳ ἐκκλησιάζουσι; πάντα ἡμῖν ὁ θεὸς προδηλοῖ καὶ προκαταγγέλλει); Origen reshapes them, so they are not put in quotation marks here. The last clause is direct speech in Greek (τό· …); rendered as indirect speech to keep double quotation marks for Celsus’s words. ‘Received the word’ (τὸν λόγον): left lower case as the Christian message, though Origen may mean the Logos himself. ‘Counterfeits’ (νόθοι, bastards) may echo Plato’s contrast of bastard and true-born students of philosophy (Republic 7.535c–536a); not certain enough to cite inline. ‘Forsaken’ (ἐγκαταλελεῖφθαι) may recall Scripture on Israel forsaken, but no specific verse is clear; uncited. καθαρούς agrees with ἡμᾶς, not with βίου: the life makes us, pure from all wickedness, his own.
